distinguishing_feature: [LLM DRAFT] Pain with manipulation of the pinna or tragus, unlike acute otitis media where the pain is internal.
[LLM DRAFT] Long-standing tympanic membrane perforation with persistent purulent discharge rather than acute fluid accumulation.
[LLM DRAFT] Generalized upper respiratory symptoms without the acute, prominent middle ear inflammation and bulging tympanic membrane.
[LLM DRAFT] Prominent tonsillar exudates and marked enlargement compared to diffuse pharyngeal inflammation
[LLM DRAFT] Concurrent prominent sneezing, nasal congestion, and cough rather than isolated sore throat
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of painful, discrete oral ulcers with erythematous halos rather than generalized pharyngeal erythema
[LLM DRAFT] Symptoms typically resolve within 7 to 10 days without worsening, unlike acute bacterial sinusitis which often shows a 'double sickening'.
[LLM DRAFT] Prominent nasal pruritus, sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea with associated allergic triggers, typically lacking purulent discharge and facial pain.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized predominantly by sore throat and pharyngeal inflammation rather than facial pressure or nasal congestion.
[LLM DRAFT] Diffuse pharyngeal mucosal inflammation and lack of prominent localized tonsillar enlargement or exudates.
[LLM DRAFT] Predominance of generalized cold symptoms like sneezing and rhinorrhea with minimal throat pain.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of painful oral ulcers on non-tonsillar mucosal surfaces rather than inflamed tonsils.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of purulent nasal discharge and facial pain or pressure rather than clear rhinorrhea and itching.
[LLM DRAFT] Self-limiting course lasting less than 10-14 days, often accompanied by systemic symptoms like fever and myalgias.
[LLM DRAFT] Dominant symptom of a painful throat with pharyngeal erythema or exudates rather than prominent nasal symptoms.
[LLM DRAFT] Diffuse pharyngeal erythema and exudates rather than discrete, painful oral ulcers.
[LLM DRAFT] Inflamed, enlarged tonsils frequently covered with purulent exudate, unlike localized canker sores.
[LLM DRAFT] Accompanied by generalized upper respiratory symptoms such as rhinorrhea and sneezing without primary painful oral ulcerations.

[LLM DRAFT] Inflammation of the external ear canal often presenting with pain upon manipulation of the pinna, whereas chronic suppurative otitis media primarily features a persistent tympanic membrane perforation and middle ear discharge.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with rapid-onset signs of middle ear inflammation and acute pain rather than a long-standing chronic tympanic membrane perforation with persistent otorrhea.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by a rhythmic, pulsing sound in the ear rather than the chronic purulent ear discharge and conductive hearing loss typical of chronic suppurative otitis media.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with rhinorrhea and sore throat rather than systemic cyanosis or severe oxygen desaturation.
[LLM DRAFT] Tympanic membrane is bulging and inflamed with normal external auditory canal.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of a tympanic membrane perforation with persistent otorrhea.
[LLM DRAFT] Perceived as a continuous ringing or buzzing rather than a synchronized heartbeat sound
[LLM DRAFT] Pulsatile noise is restricted to the left side rather than present bilaterally
[LLM DRAFT] Pulsatile noise is restricted to the right side rather than present bilaterally
[LLM DRAFT] Pulsatile sound perceived exclusively in the contralateral (right) ear rather than the left.
[LLM DRAFT] Pulsatile sound perceived synchronously in both ears rather than localized solely to the left ear.
[LLM DRAFT] Pulsatile tinnitus described without lateralization to a specific ear, requiring clinical determination of left-sided involvement.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with a synchronized whooshing sound in both ears rather than being localized exclusively to the right side.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with a vascular or rhythmic sound localized specifically to the left ear instead of the right.
[LLM DRAFT] Lacks the specific lateralization to the right ear noted in the primary presentation.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with synchronized rhythmic ringing perceived in both ears simultaneously, often prompting evaluation for systemic or intracranial vascular causes.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by a rhythmic, pulse-synchronous sound localized specifically to the left ear, requiring exclusion of left-sided carotid or jugular pathology.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with a heartbeat-synchronous sound restricted to the right ear, necessitating targeted imaging of the right temporal bone and associated vasculature.
[LLM DRAFT] Erythema and exudates on the posterior pharynx without prominent tonsillar enlargement
[LLM DRAFT] Inflammation primarily localized to the palatine tonsils often with visible purulent exudate
[LLM DRAFT] Concurrent prominent nasal congestion and sneezing preceding or accompanying the throat discomfort
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of a rhythmic, heartbeat-synchronized sound rather than a continuous tone.
[LLM DRAFT] Localization of the ringing to a single ear rather than affecting both symmetrically.
[LLM DRAFT] Associated chronic otorrhea, tympanic membrane perforation, and persistent purulent drainage.
[LLM DRAFT] Right-sided ringing or hissing noise instead of left-sided perception.
[LLM DRAFT] Ringing or hissing noise perceived in both ears simultaneously.
[LLM DRAFT] The ringing sound in the left ear has a rhythmic, beating quality synchronized with the heartbeat.
[LLM DRAFT] Tinnitus is localized to the contralateral ear rather than the right ear.
[LLM DRAFT] Tinnitus is perceived bilaterally rather than exclusively in the right ear.
[LLM DRAFT] Tinnitus has a rhythmic, pulse-synchronous quality rather than a steady tone in the right ear.
[LLM DRAFT] Perceived ringing or buzzing sound reported in both ears simultaneously.
[LLM DRAFT] Auditory sensation of a rhythmic pulsing or throbbing synchronous with the heartbeat.
[LLM DRAFT] Associated with persistent purulent otorrhea and tympanic membrane perforation.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of prominent tonsillar exudates and marked inflammation focused primarily on the palatine tonsils.
[LLM DRAFT] More diffuse inflammation of the posterior pharynx without prominent localized tonsillar enlargement or exudate.
[LLM DRAFT] Symptom profile dominated by prominent rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and sneezing rather than severe isolated throat pain.
[LLM DRAFT] Prominent pharyngeal inflammation and pain rather than generalized upper respiratory congestion.
[LLM DRAFT] Facial pain and pressure lasting beyond 10 days or worsening after initial improvement.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of prominent pruritus, sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea without systemic symptoms like fever.
